Chapter 2: The Body’s Instincts and the Roots of Trauma.
Now, building on the idea that trauma really lives in the body, let’s explore how our nervous system responds whenever it senses a threat.
Think about it—our bodies come equipped with an amazing set of survival tools, passed down from our ancestors and shared with the animal kingdom. You’ve probably heard of these before: fight, flight, and freeze. These aren’t choices we make; they’re automatic, designed to give us the best shot at making it through danger.
The moment your body picks up on a threat, everything changes. Your muscles tense up, breathing gets faster, and suddenly, your focus narrows to just what’s in front of you. If you can run or defend yourself, your body makes that happen. But if escape isn’t an option, you might freeze—almost like hitting a pause button. And here’s something important: this freeze response isn’t about giving up. It’s actually a last-ditch effort from your body to survive when things feel overwhelming.
In the wild, animals handle this pretty seamlessly. After a close call, they’ll literally shake off all that pent-up energy and go right back to normal. But for us humans, it’s not always that simple. Social pressures, fear of losing control, or just not knowing what’s happening can make us suppress these natural responses. The result? That survival energy has nowhere to go—it just builds up inside.
And that trapped energy? It’s really at the core of trauma symptoms. You might notice it as chronic tension, feeling emotionally numb, sudden panic attacks, or even a sense of being cut off from the world around you. Your nervous system stays revved up, acting like the threat is still there. So, everyday situations can set off reactions that feel way too intense for what’s actually happening.
Here’s a helpful way to picture it: imagine your nervous system is like a thermostat. When everything’s working right, it adjusts smoothly and keeps things balanced. But when trauma throws it off, it’s like the thermostat gets stuck—either blasting on high, which we call hyperarousal, or shutting down completely. The whole point of healing is to bring back that natural flexibility.
Let’s make this real. Think of someone who had a serious accident as a child. Even years later, a loud noise might leave them feeling jumpy or on edge. Or maybe someone feels strangely numb after a medical procedure, not really sure why. These reactions aren’t random—they’re the body’s way of handling survival energy that never got a chance to finish its cycle.
Understanding these patterns can change everything. Instead of seeing symptoms as problems to get rid of, what if we viewed them as messages? Signals from the body, telling us what needs care and attention. Healing is about learning to listen to those signals, and gently supporting your body to complete the responses it started long ago.
